issues.legal_issue: A writ petitioner cannot relitigate a matter already decided, or a matter that could and ought to have been raised in the earlier proceeding.
material_facts: The challenged acquisition and the contention that the land fell outside the project agreement had been litigated in earlier proceedings.
The Supreme Court had previously rejected the contention that land beyond the main road alignment was outside the integrated project and had upheld the acquisition.
The appellant knew the contents of the project agreement and could have raised the relevant contention in the earlier proceedings but gave no reasonable explanation for not doing so.
The appellant brought a further writ proceeding raising the same acquisition issues.
issues.conclusion: The renewed challenge was barred by res judicata and constructive res judicata; those principles apply to writ petitions, and the further proceeding was also an abuse of the process of the court.
issues.legal_principle: Constructive res judicata under Explanation IV to Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies to writ petitions. An adjudication is conclusive not only as to matters actually decided but also as to matters that the parties might and ought to have litigated as part of the same controversy. The Court relied on State of Karnataka v. All India Manufacturers Organisation, Direct Recruit Class II Engineering Officers' Association v. State of Maharashtra, State of U.P. v. Nawab Hussain, Devilal Modi v. Sales Tax Officer, Daryao v. State of U.P., Greenhalgh v. Mallard, and Sheoparsan Singh v. Rammanandan Prasad Singh. Relitigation may also be an abuse of process even when it is not technically barred by res judicata, as explained in K.K. Modi v. K.N. Modi.

rule.if: writ_challenge and prior_final_adjudication and (same_issue_decided or omitted_issue_could_and_ought_to_have_been_raised) and no_reason_for_omission

predicates.writ_challenge: A party brings a writ proceeding to challenge a matter previously litigated.
predicates.prior_final_adjudication: A competent court has finally adjudicated an earlier proceeding concerning the matter.
predicates.same_issue_decided: The issue raised in the later proceeding was decided in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.omitted_issue_could_and_ought_to_have_be: The later issue was part of the earlier controversy and could and ought to have been raised there.
predicates.no_reason_for_omission: The party offers no reasonable explanation for not raising the issue in the earlier proceeding.

issues.definition: When a writ challenge follows a final adjudication, a decided issue or an unexplained issue that could and ought to have been raised cannot be litigated again.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of an award within the period prescribed for awards under the general land acquisition law does not lapse an acquisition under a separate enactment when that enactment provides for vesting on publication of the acquisition declaration.
material_facts: The appellant contended that the acquisition had lapsed because no award was made within two years of the acquisition notification.
Under the applicable enactment, publication of the acquisition declaration vested the land in the State free from encumbrances.
The applicable enactment did not make vesting dependent on an award, and the Court treated it as a self-contained code with purposes distinct from the general land acquisition law.
issues.conclusion: The award-period provision in the general land acquisition law did not apply to the acquisition, which had vested on publication of the declaration, and the acquisition had not lapsed for want of an award within that period.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished the vesting mechanism under Sections 28(4) and 28(5) of the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act from vesting under Section 16 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Where the special enactment provides that land vests on publication of the declaration, vesting does not depend on an award and the award-period provision in Section 11A of the 1894 Act does not cause the acquisition to lapse. The Court relied on Pratap v. State of Rajasthan, Munithimmaiah v. State of Karnataka, Offshore Holdings Pvt. Ltd. v. Bangalore Development Authority, and Girnar Traders v. State of Maharashtra. It distinguished Mariyappa v. State of Karnataka because the enactment considered there was not a self-contained code and was supplemental to the general acquisition law.

predicates.special_statutory_acquisition: The proceeding concerns acquisition under a special statutory enactment rather than acquisition solely under the general land acquisition law.
predicates.declaration_publication_vests_land_indep: The special enactment provides that publication of the acquisition declaration vests the land without requiring an award.

issues.definition: An acquisition under a special enactment that vests land upon publication of its declaration does not lapse merely because an award is not made within the general award period.

issues.legal_issue: A court may impose costs and protect completion of a public project when a further appeal re-agitates finally rejected challenges as an abuse of process aimed at obstructing the project.
material_facts: The appellant pursued a further appeal after the acquisition had been upheld in earlier proceedings, including by the Supreme Court.
The further proceeding repeated issues already rejected and sought to hold up the acquisition and project.
The project had been upheld as an integrated project serving a larger public purpose.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the appeal was an abuse of the process of the court, dismissed it with costs, and directed the State to complete the project without releasing acquired land in a way that could impede completion.
issues.legal_principle: Court process must be used bona fide and properly; relitigation of an issue already tried and decided may be an abuse of process, contrary to justice and public policy, whether or not it is independently barred by res judicata. The Court relied on K.K. Modi v. K.N. Modi and State of Karnataka v. All India Manufacturers Organisation, and applied the principle that public interest in a validated project may justify directions preventing its obstruction.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: A party brings an appeal concerning a project or acquisition previously adjudicated.
predicates.relitigation_of_finally_rejected_issues: The appellant raises issues that a court has already considered and rejected in earlier proceedings.
predicates.attempt_to_obstruct_validated_public_pro: The further proceeding is used to delay or impede a public project that has been judicially upheld.

issues.definition: When an appeal repeats rejected issues in an attempt to impede a judicially upheld public project, the court may impose costs and protect completion of the project.
